decisions.mark: concludes that the DENY list is the only one that blocks execution — ServerManager's execute path consults is_denied and nothing else before routing the call
decisions.detail: QUOTE: NONE | WHY: The answer says two checks decide execution (approval in ToolExecutor, then deny in ServerManager), not that the deny list is the only blocker, and ServerManager's execute path is described as consulting is_denied only after an approval layer that can refuse calls.

decisions.mark: states that the ALLOW list does not grant execution but suppresses the approval step — it is consulted only from ToolExecutor::check_approval, in a different file
decisions.detail: QUOTE: "A deny match also overrides `auto_approve` and the allow list, because it is checked unconditionally in `execute`." | WHY: The answer shows the allow list inside `check_approval` and the deny list in `ServerManager::execute`. It never says the allow list only suppresses the approval step without granting execution, or that it is consulted only from `check_approval`. The most it does is imply this through the deny-override remark.

decisions.mark: concludes that the effective posture is default-ALLOW at the blocking gate — a tool matching neither list is not denied and runs
decisions.detail: QUOTE: NONE | WHY: The answer never concludes that a tool matching neither list runs by default; its flow shows "otherwise → Permission denied" at the approval layer, and it says nothing about default-allow at the blocking gate.

decisions.mark: identifies that the approval callback CANNOT refuse — it returns void, and the code sets approved to true unconditionally after firing it
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `check_approval` fires `on_tool_call` and then sets `approved = true` without reading a return value. With a callback registered, every call passes the approval layer. | WHY: The answer states the callback is fired and approval is then set true unconditionally, so it cannot refuse. It doesn't mention the void return type, but the unconditional-approval mechanism is stated.

decisions.mark: explains that a pattern is matched with fnmatch, split at the first colon into a tool part and an argument part, and that a pattern with no colon matches on the tool name alone
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `PermissionManager::pattern_matches` (`src/mcp/permission_manager.cpp:101`) splits each pattern at the first `:`; table: "`filesystem.read_file` | fnmatch against the tool name | (none) | Every call to that tool, any args" | WHY: The answer says patterns are split at the first colon into a tool part (fnmatch against the tool name) and an argument part, and that a pattern with no colon matches every call to that tool, so it matches on the tool name alone.

decisions.mark: states that only ONE argument value ever reaches the pattern — the rest of the call's arguments are invisible to permission matching, and a non-string or unparseable argument collapses to a wildcard
decisions.detail: QUOTE: "The right side is matched against the tool name plus the first string value in the args JSON (`ServerManager::args_to_pattern`, `server_manager.cpp:426`). Empty args, `{}`, or a non-string first value all become `*`." | WHY: The answer says only the first string argument value reaches the pattern and that empty or non-string first values collapse to `*`. That covers the single-value and wildcard-collapse parts. It does not state outright that the other arguments are invisible to matching, but that follows directly from only the first being matched.
